section_title: What is the difference between true gain and chasing wealth?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 3 If anyone teaches another doctrine and disagrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with godly teaching, 4 he is conceited and understands nothing. Instead, he has an unhealthy interest in controversies and disputes about words, out of which come envy, strife, abusive talk, evil suspicions, 5 and constant friction between men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth. These men regard godliness as a means of gain.

6 Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. 7 For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. 8 But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these.

9 Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. 10 For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.

context_lines: Paul returns to teaching that departs from Jesus and the godly life. He describes its fruit: pride, disputes, suspicion and friction. At the center is an attempt to turn religion into a source of profit.

He then turns the idea of gain around. A faithful life joined with contentment is great gain, because possessions cannot follow us beyond death. Food and clothing give him a concrete way to speak about enough, rather than an endless demand for more.

The Greek word for contentment, [autarkeia](https://biblehub.com/greek/841.htm) (ow-TAR-kay-ah), describes being satisfied with one’s lot. The word for love of money, [philargyria](https://biblehub.com/greek/5365.htm) (fil-ar-goo-REE-ah), names greed for money. Paul’s warning concerns that craving, which can draw people from the faith into harmful choices and deep sorrow. Verse 17 will address wealthy believers directly, so possessing money and loving money are not treated as the same thing.
common_interpretation_lines: [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/1_timothy/6.htm) and [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-timothy/) both read this as a serious warning against greed and a call to contentment. Calvin explains that Paul is describing the many evils money-love produces, rather than claiming that every sin has this one cause. Neither reads godliness as a promise that believers will become wealthy.

Traditions differ over how departure from faith relates to final salvation. The Reformed [Westminster Confession 17](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html) teaches that those truly saved will be preserved, though they may fall seriously. The [Methodist Articles, Article XII](https://www.umc.org/en/content/articles-of-religion), allow that a person may depart from grace and also return through God’s grace. Both approaches take the warning seriously; they differ over whether a truly saved person can finally fall away.
god_plan_lines: In [Luke 12:15–21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/12.htm), Jesus tells of a man who builds up his possessions but is unprepared to meet God. The parallel is the mistake of treating stored wealth as lasting security.

[Matthew 6:19–24](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/6.htm) places treasure, the heart and serving God together. These passages widen Paul’s warning: God is forming people whose deepest hope and loyalty rest in Him, beyond what they can accumulate in this life.
